one_liner: Pure-Go seeded 64-bit hash from Abseil's wyhash-style design; beats seeded XXH3 5-13% at 4-128 B, 1.4-1.8x at 192-256 B.
what_it_does: A small Go package with three one-shot functions: Hash64([]byte, seed), Hash64String(string, seed) and Hash64Uint64x2(a, b, seed). Each returns a 64-bit CircleHash64f digest. It is built for short keys (the author says <=512 bytes) that need a seeded, deterministic digest that stays the same across processes and releases; the v0.3.0 release notes declare CircleHash64f digests stable. It is a different algorithm from XXH3, so digests differ. It has no hash.Hash64/streaming interface and no 128-bit output.
how_it_is_fast: Every mixing step is the wyhash/Abseil multiply-fold: a 64x64->128-bit multiply via math/bits.Mul64, with the high and low halves XORed together. Tails use overlapping unaligned reads (two 4-byte reads for 4-8 B, two 8-byte reads for 9-16 B, three single bytes for 1-3 B), so there are no per-byte loops. Inputs of 64 bytes or less go through a separate function that has only a 16-byte loop. Longer inputs run a 64-byte loop with four independent multiplies over two state lanes. It is plain Go with no assembly: the Go 1.17+ file reads words through unsafe pointers using little-endian byte shifts, and a build-tagged reference file covers older Go.
when_to_use: Pure-Go code without cgo that hashes short keys (mostly <=256 bytes) and needs a seeded 64-bit digest that is identical across processes, machines and library versions, for example on-disk hash-ordered maps or persistent indexes. onflow/atree, the Flow blockchain's storage layer, uses it this way and falls back to BLAKE3 on collisions.
Replacing SipHash as the seeded hash in a Go hash structure: the README table shows 3.7-6.8x SipHash's throughput at 4-256 B.
Hashing pairs of uint64 (composite IDs, slab/index pairs) with Hash64Uint64x2, without building a byte slice. The digest equals Hash64 of the 16-byte little-endian encoding.

Teams that must audit their hash: about 200 lines of optimized Go plus a 129-line reference implementation, pi-derived constants, and compatibility tests over roughly 600,000 digests on 0-16384-byte inputs.
when_not_to_use: Hashes that never leave the process, such as in-memory Go maps and sets. The runtime map and hash/maphash already handle those with per-process random seeds. CircleHash's niche is the case maphash cannot cover, because maphash seeds cannot be serialized or recreated in another process.

Keys an attacker can choose, or anywhere HashDoS resistance matters. The seed does not prevent seed-independent multicollisions (see gotchas). The CircleHash64fx variant meant to fix this, which also adds a 128-bit seed, has been an open, unpublished issue (#15) since March 2022.

Bulk data or inputs well above 512 bytes. The author says CircleHash64 is ideal for <=512 B and publishes no numbers above 256 B, and there is no SIMD path. XXH3's SIMD long-input code is the better fit there.

Codebases outside Go. There is no official C, C++ or Rust port, and porters have asked for simple known-answer test vectors with data (issue #23, open since 2022) because the published tests only check SHA-512 checksums over thousands of digests.
Anything that needs 128-bit digests: CircleHash128fx (issue #16) is also unpublished.

integration.dependencies: none (Go standard library only: math/bits, unsafe)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.17 for the optimized path (go.mod: go 1.17); a build-tagged reference implementation serves Go 1.16 and older. CI tests Go 1.17 and 1.22-1.25.
integration.platforms: Only linux_amd64 is officially supported per the README, though CI also runs macOS, Ubuntu and Windows. The code is pure Go and builds words from bytes in little-endian order, so digests should not depend on host endianness.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. The API is stateless pure functions with no mutable package-level state (from source), so concurrent calls should be safe.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the call shape matches a one-shot seeded 64-bit XXH3 call (bytes or string plus a uint64 seed returns a uint64), but digests differ, so every persisted hash changes. There is no streaming/hash.Hash64 interface and no 128-bit variant.

gotchas: Multiply-by-zero weakness, confirmed with a Python port of the source that matches the repo's 65,536-digest known-answer checksum: when an 8-byte little-endian word that is XORed with the constant pi1 (0x13198A2E03707344) equals pi1, the product is zero. Every 9-16-byte input whose first 8 bytes are pi1 hashes to 0 under every seed, including Hash64Uint64x2(pi1, x, seed). A 16-byte block that starts with pi1 also erases all earlier input and the seed, so same-length inputs that share everything after that block collide for all seeds. The README describes CircleHash64fx as the fix, but fx is not shipped.

The README says CircleHash64fx 'will replace CircleHash64f as the default', and issue #25 plans an API refactor before v1.0. Hash64 is documented as CircleHash64f-compatible, so pin v0.3.0 and add a regression test on digests if they are persisted (onflow/atree does both).

Methodology: no Benchmark functions are published. The README table's XXH3 implementation is unnamed; the author's earlier atree#103 evaluation used github.com/zeebo/xxh3. The table's XXH3 throughput falls from 11.6 GB/s at 128 B to 8.19 GB/s at 256 B, which accounts for most of the headline 1.83x. The author's atree write-up says such slowdowns at larger sizes 'are not a typo'.
The Go 1.17+ file uses unsafe pointer arithmetic to read slice and string data. Hash64 on a nil or empty slice is safe because no bytes are read.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it when you are in pure Go and need a stable, seeded, persistable 64-bit digest of short keys without cgo. wyhash and xxHash/XXH3 are the C originals of the same ideas; in C or C++ use them directly, or rapidhash, which has a Rust port. In Rust, foldhash, aHash and rapidhash are the in-language choices and are the better fits there.
verified_claims_summary: The claim is the author's README table, repeated in the v0.2.0 release notes, which add that it came from `go test -bench=. -count=20` plus benchstat. It shows seeded CircleHash64f at 1.34-15.0 GB/s against an unnamed seeded XXH3 at 1.21-8.19 GB/s on 4-256-byte inputs, under Go 1.17.7 on darwin_amd64 with an Intel i7-1068NG7. That works out to 1.05-1.13x at 4-128 B and 1.44x/1.83x at 192/256 B. The benchmark code is not published, and the rurban/smhasher README has no CircleHash row, so the speed and SMHasher-pass claims are first-party only.
status_note: The algorithm and code are frozen since v0.3.0 (March 2022; the last source edit was lint in August 2024), and 2025-2026 commits are dependabot/CI bumps. Still, it is Apache-2.0 with zero dependencies, digests are declared stable, and it runs in production in onflow/atree and the wider Flow Go stack, so depending on or vendoring v0.3.0 is low-risk. The promised fx and 128-bit variants remain unpublished.
